learnings: LiveKit gates every latency view behind a free Observability toggle; once on, the Agents page gains Response Latency 'tails by stage' and Interrupted Rate — stage-level latency is the norm (sip-agents-observability-panels).

Retell puts the Disconnection Reason next to End-to-End latency in the call's analysis block and exposes per-turn E2E latency only as log lines — nobody attributes latency per leg (carrier vs platform vs model) (sip-call-detail-*).

Vapi is the only vendor that budgets latency per leg on the assistant page (Transcriber 100 ms · Model 600 ms · Voice 200 ms) and names every failure with an endedReason value — but the call detail's Latency Summary shows 0 turns / 0 ms for a failed call instead of saying why (sip-assistant-latency-per-leg, sip-call-latency-summary-zero-turns).

ElevenLabs attributes latency at one leg only — a per-turn 'LLM 723 ms' badge in the transcript — while its Audio dashboard defines a fuller taxonomy (Agent Response Time / Response Generation / Turn Taking) that stayed empty after a real conversation (sip-conversation-transcript-llm-latency, sip-dashboard-audio-latency-empty).

ElevenLabs' SIP docs give explicit carrier-vs-us fault signatures (BYE/481, one-way audio, G711/G722 mismatch) and split latency into model inference · time-to-first-audio · network round-trip — the vocabulary our verdicts should use (elevenlabs-sip-troubleshooting, elevenlabs-sip-understanding-latency).
Retell's analytics default range renders all-zero KPIs with no empty state, so 0 ms reads as 'fine'; our empty states must say 'no calls in range' (sip-analytics-empty-default-range).

LiveKit's Telephony page has a 'Calls with issues' panel and SIP trunks as first-class objects; the inbound trunk form carries SRTP, headers and Krisp (sip-telephony-calls-empty, sip-trunk-inbound-form).

Whitespace: no vendor draws a signalling ladder or names the responsible party. SW4Y4M's verdict + 'Attributed to' is ahead of the market — it needs time on the ladder and a fix per verdict to become the diagnostic.

shot.alt: Monitor › Live calls — issues first, with the reason on the row, marked in red

rows.rationale: A Live calls tab on Monitor: what is in progress, with the calls that have gone wrong sorted to the top and the reason written on the row in the caller's words. The clock names its own lag and can be paused, so a row can be read without sliding away. The concurrency wall is named when callers start holding. Opening a call gives four verbs taken from the only documented set in the field: listen, put words in, take over, end. The two a caller would notice are confirmed, and taking over mutes the agent on the same tick rather than at the end of its sentence.
rows.next: OWNER DECISION, and the one thing that can change this design: which verbs are permitted, and for whom. All four are built. Listening changes nothing for the caller; taking over and ending are the ones that need a role behind them.

secondary.label: Live call control — say, mute-assistant, end-call, listen
secondary.note: The only documented set of operator verbs in the field, and it has no interface on top of it.

rainy.jtbd: Calls exceed my concurrency; new callers must get a clear outcome and I must be alerted.

learnings: Retell has the right table and the wrong order: sorted by start time, it cannot answer which of forty calls needs a person.
LiveKit is alone in naming the lag, with an Auto-refresh toggle on its sessions list. A row that slides away while it is read is worse than one that is a few seconds old and says so.
Vapi documents the verbs and ships no interface for them: say, add-message, mute-assistant, end-call, transfer, handoff, plus a listen socket.
Retell shows concurrency used against the cap in its sidebar, so the wall is visible before callers start holding.

B · Issues first, only the calls that have gone wrong
C · A dock that follows you across every page
D · Verbs behind a role, listen for everyone
E · Watch only, no operator verbs at all

C is a follow-up once there is a reason to watch a call while doing something else; D is the open owner question, because who may take over is a permissions decision rather than a design one; E fails the job outright.

rows.name: 13 · Dashboards & alerts

rows.jtbd: User wants to see agent health without asking an engineer.

shot.alt: Monitor › Overview: Answered calls carries its own Watch control, so the threshold is set where the number is read · marked in red

rows.rationale: A threshold is a property of the number it watches, so the watch rides the tile and there is no Alerts tab: a rules page needs a metric picker, and a picker is where first contact resolution and answer speed come back as numbers Agora cannot compute. The tile set underneath is rebuilt from the contract, so four watchable numbers survive (total calls, answered calls, answer rate for outbound, handle time), answer speed keeps a row and reads Requires Engine, the outcome ring becomes two counts that sum to the call total, and first contact resolution, sentiment and the success tile get no row at all. On a count tile the condition list holds No calls at all, which is the one rule a threshold on a rate can never carry, so a trunk refusing every call fires instead of reading as a quiet Sunday. A watch knows a number crossed a line and not why, so the breach borrows the diagnosis already running on that deployment and its Fix opens the setting that caused it, and when no cause was found the card offers the calls rather than a Fix button with nothing behind it. Delivery stays where delivery lives, with one new row in Project notifications, because two doors for one action is the thing this design refuses.
rows.next: OWNER DECISION: who owns the sentence that defines success? Today the headline success number is whatever an LLM prompt typed into a box on one phone number decides. Keep it and a watch on it watches four different sentences, and its breach cannot name what broke; define it once in Studio and the per-number prompt becomes an override plus a backend ask. Until that is answered the success tile stays off the screen and only the four tiles that do not depend on it ship. Not built: any group-by, because it needs labels written when the agent joins the channel and labels is excluded from the configurable set; no dashboard builder, no saved views, no sentiment, no first contact resolution tile, ever, until someone writes the formula. Requires Engine, named on screen rather than drawn around: answer speed, alert delivery receipts, the turn batch (event 112), an OpenTelemetry payload, and per-call evidence beyond 7 days.

secondary.label: Alerting › Create Alert, the rule as one sentence
secondary.note: Retell writes the rule as a sentence made of two selects and a typed value, Check every 5 min for the last 30 min, with Compare to certain value or to last cycle, and it costs them the link back to the chart the user was staring at, because the analytics range and the alert window never meet.

secondary.label: Alerting list, empty, over four editable templates
secondary.note: Retell answers the empty alerting list with four ready-made rules a user can edit into their own rather than a drawing of a bell, and it costs them a metric catalogue that has to carry every watchable number in one picker, in a place away from the tiles.

secondary.label: Monitoring: monitors, triggers, issues and notifiers over an Insight
secondary.note: Vapi builds the alert on the same saved Insight a board renders, so the chart and the rule read one query, and it costs them a raw cron field, an issue.created with no second event to say it is over, and monitors that need retained call data and stay silent until the targeted assistants have calls.

secondary.label: Home dashboard over Last 90 days, tabbed with user-created views
secondary.note: ElevenLabs ships the richest reading surface of the four, tabs plus Create view plus per-chart scale switches, and it costs them any alert at all: there is no threshold, no rule and no recipient anywhere in the product, and each tab silently keeps its own date range.

secondary.label: Evaluation tab, empty because the criteria are upstream
secondary.note: ElevenLabs names the dependency in the empty state, no evaluation criteria means no chart, and it costs them a reader who cannot tell from the dashboard which agents were excluded or why the number went flat.

secondary.label: Agents observability dashboard, every panel with no data
secondary.note: LiveKit names the range as the reason its panels are blank, No data for the selected time range, and puts Interrupted rate and E2E median on the front page, and it costs them the next move entirely: there is no alert, no threshold and no destination anywhere in the console, so observability is read-only.

rows.verdict: Verdict: B on C, scored 31 against A's 11 over 24 rainy scenarios and 5 learnings, with D shipped in the same commit as one event list replaced and two rows added, and E rejected at 1 point.
learnings: The alert rule is a threshold added to a tile, not a second form in a second place: Vapi's trigger references the same Insight a board renders, and Retell's rule reuses the Post Call Extraction filters its charts use.

The rule form is two selects and a number, and it must ship its own all-clear: Retell publishes eight window and frequency pairs, two comparison modes, a cap of 10 rules per workspace and a Resolved email, while Vapi's raw cron is the part not to copy.

The customer's own post-call field is the group-by, which is how sentiment and success ship without waiting on Engine, because Vapi exposes it as column, groupBy and filter and Retell lets any extraction field drive a chart.

Trace export is a format select on the webhook we already ship, not a destination catalogue: ElevenLabs turns a workspace webhook into an OTLP exporter with one toggle and LiveKit does it with two environment variables and no screen.

Every tile needs a definition line, because no voice vendor defines a single one of the five inbound pilot metrics, while Amazon Connect publishes a formula page per metric and splits contact-record from agent-activity numbers on purpose.
directions: A · Alerts as a sixth tab
B · The threshold rides the tile (chosen)
C · Name the number before you watch it
D · Watch it from your own tools
E · A dashboard you can build

rows.name: 14 · Evals & scorecards

shot.alt: Go live › Scorecard, empty on a new agent · one named list replaces the grading sentence that was written in two places with opposite defaults, marked in red

rows.rationale: One named list of checks replaces the same grading sentence written in two places with opposite defaults, and a criterion is the same record a test assertion is, so the sentence that grades a draft run and the sentence that would grade a real call cannot drift. The run half ships whole: the suite survives the tab, a text run repeats three times and the row carries the rate rather than one roll of the dice, and a case you wrote yourself finally returns a result instead of an empty sheet. What the design refuses to do is score a production call, because Agora keeps no transcript for a finished one, so Call Outcome stops printing a verdict the product never computed and names what is missing instead. It also refuses a second table, a second column beside Call Outcome, a scorecards library and any write back into a live agent: one editor, one door, and a failure that names the setting to fix rather than changing it behind the user. The price of that honesty is a column reading Not scored on every row until the stored transcript lands.
rows.next: OWNER DECISION: Call Outcome has printed a value the product never computed for months and this build stops printing it, so do we keep the column with Not scored and its reason on every row, or take it out of the table and off the filter until it can be answered? Keeping it leaves a column customers already sort by carrying one honest state and keeps the dependency visible; removing it takes away a filter they have today and hides that dependency, and either way it is the column owner's call. Not built: no per-criterion verdict, reason or count on a real call, no compare row against the version callers are on, no recording review, no CLI or CI door, and no self-improving write. The stored transcript for a finished call, the recording and any judge on Agora's side are all Requires Engine, so the call half ships as its named dependency and nothing more.

learnings: Vapi has already migrated off the exact control we ship, telling new users to replace the free-text success prompt with a reusable object plus a scorecard because structured outputs are where new development happens.

Both vendors who score real calls report a result and a reason per criterion: Retell names which metrics passed and which failed with a reason for each, and ElevenLabs returns success, failure or unknown with a rationale across up to 30 criteria.
ElevenLabs runs one test 2 to 20 times and badges the pass rate, on its own stated grounds that a single pass shows an agent can succeed while a rate shows how often it will.
Retell prices the grading itself at $0.10 per analyzed minute after 100 free minutes, on a page that opens by saying there is no separate test tier and no free testing sandbox.

A self-improving agent ships at exactly one vendor and it never writes on its own: Retell's Conductor puts every edit behind Accept change or Reject change, and anything left unaccepted is rejected on submit.
rows.verdict: Verdict: C, with one honest side. A criterion is an assertion with a name, so the checks that grade a draft run and the checks that would grade a real call are one record and cannot drift. The run half ships whole, because Studio owns a test transcript at the moment it makes one: named criteria, a stored run, a repeat count and a rate, and an authored case that finally returns a result. The call half ships as its stated dependency, because Agora keeps no transcript for a finished call, so every per-criterion verdict, reason and count on the calls list would have been invented. A's deletion of the second criteria box survives whole, B's per-criterion call reporting waits on that Engine row, D folds away until a second agent needs the same sentence, and E gives up its one door, Save as test on a real call.

shot.alt: One table is the suite, Type on every row: the Test table with Test Name, Type and Status, every generated row typed Conversation and Not Run, marked in red

rows.rationale: One table stays the suite, and the seam engineering describes rides the row as a Type: a Decision check asks whether the agent made the right next move, a Conversation asks whether it reached the right outcome. It refuses the second test section that Vapi and LiveKit put in their nav, because the line those two actually draw is turn level against whole conversation, and in both of them audio is a mode inside one object, never a surface of its own. So text and audio are one suite run two ways: the mode is picked at the moment of spending, priced on the button as Run with audio · ~15 min · ~$1.48, and stamped on every verdict, so a pass that only proves the words can never wear the badge of a pass that was heard. The Add case sheet asks the type before it asks anything else and says out loud whether the tools are mocked, because a test that books a real appointment is the one failure nobody forgives. Regenerate no longer throws authored work away, and the Go live pre-flight reports which machine produced the pass instead of showing a silent tick.
rows.next: OWNER DECISION: does Send a custom instruction return text, or does it only speak? If it answers in text, a Decision check can run against the real agent rather than a mock of it, which no competitor offers today, and the type blurb drops the word mock. If it only speaks, Decision checks stay a separate text runner and the copy has to say so on every row. Requires Engine: the audio mode is the voice simulation runtime, so the prototype times a mock call and prices it from the $0.10 an agent minute rate. Not built: no export or identifier that runs this suite from the API or CLI, which the P0 eval ticket requires; no comparison of two runs; and no queue or progress for a batch that outlives the tab, so a thirty call audio run still assumes someone is watching. Generated scenarios also still belong to the mount that produced them, so a Generate in the Test section leaves the rail empty, while authored cases, deletions and verdicts do share.

secondary.note: Vapi runs Evals and Simulations as two nav items and reduces the difference to did the agent make the right next decision against did it reach the right outcome, which costs a new user a comparison table to read before they can author anything.

rows.verdict: Verdict: C, with D's second home taken as a graft. One suite, every case typed Decision check or Conversation, every run moded text or audio and priced where the money is spent, and the long batched run given a home next to the Go live pre-flight. A is rejected even though two of four vendors split, because they split turn level from whole conversation and keep audio as a mode inside one object, so copying their number of surfaces while ignoring where they drew the line would look validated and be wrong. E is the right shape once runs are slow and plural, and premature as the first move.
learnings: Nobody splits text from audio, they split turn level from whole conversation: Vapi and LiveKit both put audio inside one object as a run mode, and 0 of 4 vendors give audio a surface of its own.

The deterministic half is a developer artefact everywhere it exists: LiveKit's is pytest in your repo and Vapi's is a JSON messages array sold on CI, so neither is a thing a non-developer authors in a console.

Simulation already means text in this market, because ElevenLabs, Retell and LiveKit all use the word for the thing without audio, so our audio has to be said out loud per run instead of carried by a section name.

Automated voice testing is still whitespace: only Vapi and LiveKit run a persona over the real audio pipeline, LiveKit's is beta and Python only, and it openly defers heavy audio testing to third parties.

Tool mocking is the part every serious vendor states out loud and we did not: ElevenLabs offers mock none, all or selected with a real-call fallback, LiveKit scopes mock_tools to a block, Vapi asserts exact toolCalls.

Two specialists split on a different axis again, because for Coval and Hamming an eval is the scoring layer rather than a test type, so three meanings of the word are in play and ours must be defined on screen.

Save a real call as a test is no longer whitespace, since ElevenLabs ships Create test from this conversation and Retell saves playground scenarios as graded cases, so keep the feature and drop the differentiation claim.

rows.rationale: Getting a number is a third branch of the sheet every other number door already opens, not a buy page: renting is the first item in the number field's own footer, so a number you rent and a number you bring stay one object behind one door. The branch is one field and a result list, because every vendor that sells numbers asks for an area code and nothing more, and a country picker can wait until there is a second country. It refuses to end on a receipt: the wait is a timestamped fact log and the last step is a test call the user places, because a line that has just provisioned still cannot take a call and the first ring is the thing this feature is judged on. It also refuses to name a price, since Agora documents no telephony charge and puts telephony in Beta free of charge, so the amount, the checkout step, the identity gate and the Monthly column came off rather than be invented, and the commit button carries a Requires Engine caption where a rate would sit. What the inventory gains instead is honest: a From cell that says where a number came from, two destructive verbs that no longer share one word, and Turning up, the state the model never had for a number that is owned and cannot answer yet.
rows.next: OWNER DECISION: the lock is still open on two questions and this build ships without either. First, what does first run become once numbers are purchasable: (a) nothing changes, Aria stays on a sandbox line and the card is still captured at minute 150, (b) first run offers Get a number as its second step and the card lands there, or (c) Agora grants one number on signup and the card lands on the second number or at minute 150, whichever comes first. The same answer decides whether the plans page's "1 phone number" and "10 phone numbers" are a bug to delete, which is what this build did, or a promise to write the spec for. Second, is a rented number a line item beside the $0.10 minutes or its own subscription with its own cycle, and does the spend cap cover it: until that lands no price may appear anywhere, which is why the commit button carries a Requires Engine caption instead of an amount and the release dialog states what happens to the digits and nothing about the money. Requires Engine, filed now: a third provider value for a number Agora sold, a provisioning state on the phone-number resource, a number search that returns country, area code, type and capabilities, and a purchase failure taxonomy with stable codes. Not built, deliberately: the checkout step, the identity fields and the card fold, all cut with the price, and the buy branch runs on a session ledger rather than a real search.

rows.verdict: Verdict: C, with D grafted and E's designable half taken now. Buy stays the third branch of the existing add sheet, one field and a result list, and it still ends on a call the user places, because that ending is the north star and the sibling branch of the same sheet already ships it. What comes off is the money: Agora's pricing page documents no telephony charge and the release notes put telephony in Beta free of charge, so no amount appears anywhere, and with the amount go the checkout step, the identity gate and the Monthly column. The inventory row still learns provenance and two destructive verbs, and a bought number now actually reaches that table through a session ledger the page reads. Aria's number becomes one number on four surfaces, named a sandbox line rather than an Agora-sold one, so the lock stays exactly as open as direction E claimed to leave it.
learnings: Provenance belongs on the row and not on a second page: Retell stamps every number retell-twilio, retell-telnyx or custom in the same response that carries the agent binding, which is exactly the third value our closed byo or twilio enum cannot express.

The purchase control is one field, so Phase 1 is a search box inside the existing add sheet rather than a new page: Vapi asks only for an area code, Retell's area_code is US only, and LiveKit searches on country code plus area code.

A bought number is not yet a working number and the list needs a word for the gap: LiveKit ships active, pending, released and offline and Vapi warns that calls will not work until activation completes, while our badge knows only Active and Unassigned.

Identity gates money everywhere it exists and every vendor makes the user find it by accident: Retell's KYC unlocks purchases but is reached by clicking a number, and Twilio wants a regulatory bundle per country and number type before it will sell one, so stating the requirement above the price is the cheapest differentiator in this feature.

Release is a money event and delete is not, so they cannot share a word: LiveKit bills the whole month on an early release, Retell stops the fee at release, and our own delete only removes the configuration from Agora.

rows.name: 17 · SIP trunk setup

rows.jtbd: User wants to connect their own carrier once and never touch it again.

shot.alt: Carrier, said once and stored: Guided setup opens on one carrier list, Twilio, Telnyx, Exotel and Another carrier with a name you type, each under its own routing noun, marked in red

rows.rationale: A trunk is a set of rows on the number that carries it, and setup is a handover said out loud: Agora's Origination URI goes out, the carrier's address, credential and allowed IP ranges come back, and the flow ends on a call the user places and answers. Quick connect keeps its name and loses its claim, because no vendor in this market provisions a trunk from a carrier API key, so the four timers and the invented pstn.telnyx.com host are gone and every step is written in the carrier's own nouns. It refuses a trunks list, because AddPhoneNumbersRequest stores address, transport, credential and allowlist per number and has no trunk id, so a second inventory would be a grouping the API cannot hold and the first shared edit would be four writes that can half-fail. It refuses a call capacity input and a masked credential with a rotation age, because nothing paces to the first and the contract never returns the second, and a control drawn over a value we cannot produce is the old fiction with better manners. What is left is one door, one detail page, and a Connection row that says whether a call has ever got through, which is where feature 11's 403 verdict now lands.
rows.next: OWNER DECISION: what is SIP Direct Connect to a user, and how does it differ from the Elastic SIP Trunk path? A different connection type means a third branch in the sheet and a type field the contract does not have; a property of an existing trunk means one badge and one metering row; sales-led means a status we report and never a thing the user turns on. It is P0 for September, its metering and audio-quality siblings are already delivered, and it ships as nothing until you answer. Second, and answerable in a sentence: do you want the carrier's stated calls per second kept on the trunk as a note now? It is cut here because nothing paces to it and the batch screen prints its own target, so on a yes it ships as one read-only line quoting the carrier and never an input. Requires Engine, and captioned as such on screen: gateway location as a stored record, SIP headers on the INVITE, and the transfer method with its no-answer fallback. Not built at all, so it is not mistaken for an omission: an Agora-enforced trunk ceiling, which is why the CPS verdict keeps its one door at batch calls and its Raise the CPS limit action is deleted rather than repointed.

learnings: No vendor provisions a trunk from a carrier API key, so Quick connect has to be a named guided path rather than an auto one: Vapi and Retell walk the user through the carrier's own portal, and ElevenLabs' Twilio SID and Token only rewrite an existing number's webhook.

The carrier is prose at all four vendors and a field at none, so the disabled Twilio select is a naming problem our own UI closes against the existing byo and twilio contract, not an enum to wait for.

The IP allowlist is an authentication mode with a stated alternative and it only ever covers signalling, so it belongs beside Username and Password, and the media half ships as the line telling the customer to allow those ports at the carrier.

Gateway region is a property of the address you were handed and never a per-number dropdown, so the field to add is which of the three published Origination URIs the customer pasted, recorded rather than routed on.

Only Retell turns the trunk ceiling into a control and it queues instead of dropping, which is the proven shape for a named exhaustion reason rather than a fix link that lands on a table with no CPS on it.
rows.verdict: B, with C's vocabulary and E's words taken as data: a trunk is a set of rows on the number that carries it, and setup is a named handover that ends on a call the user places. It answers seventeen of the twenty-one rainy scenarios and learnings on screen, against three for A, which wins only the happy path, and ten for D, which hands a full set of green ticks to a trunk that has never carried a call. C is the better model of reality and the worse model of what the contract can store, so its object survives as vocabulary and its inventory does not. Three hostile audits then attacked the values inside B and none proposed another direction, so the direction stands and the plan was rewritten: no fabricated credential age, no signalling IP copy button, no call capacity input.

rows.rationale: The lock holds: one agent answers on one channel, so the pick stays two surface cards and the two channels Agora cannot serve arrive as live rows underneath, each stating what it needs and recording the ask at the control instead of promising itself soon. The design refuses a fourth surface card for a channel with no API, and refuses to give that channel a page, because a page for something Agora cannot serve can only redirect back to the page it was opened from, which is the defect this feature starts from. It also refuses to draw the carrier review queue, the origin allowlist and any word that claims traffic, because no contract produces a submission, a reviewer, an origin check or a call count, and a state nothing can compute is the bare comma in better clothes. One readiness vocabulary derives from the types that already exist rather than minting a seventh, so inventory rows come from the numbers and deployments on record and the invented WhatsApp line with its own sender, agent and call count stops reaching the page. The part worth arguing about is whether naming WhatsApp and SMS at a live control is honesty or an advertisement, and the answer here is that the ask is the count that argues the Engine tickets into existence.
rows.next: OWNER DECISION: who owns the embeddable widget bundle, and which taxonomy wins. On the bundle, three answers change one string on the web surface: Agora hosts it and the action stays Copy embed code; we ship a React component on agora-agent-client-toolkit-react and the action becomes an install; or neither, and the action becomes the Embed Agent REST snippet Studio already documents. The correction ships either way, because the fake package name and the 404 CDN URL come out in the first slice whatever the answer is. On taxonomy, this build derives from ChannelKind and migrates one label rather than declaring a seventh type, and deliberately leaves session-trace's CHANNEL_LABEL alone, so Monitor can still say Chat where a deployment row says WhatsApp; collapsing that costs a rename across Sessions and Monitor and belongs to whoever owns those surfaces. Not built, and named so nothing reads as finished: WhatsApp messages and calls, SMS, removing the voice leg for a text-only agent, origin enforcement and the hosted widget bundle are all Requires Engine, with no field at any version, so they ship as rows that state the dependency and count the ask. Also not built, cut on the honesty floor: the in review and rejected states with their dates and reasons, the allowed sites list, and No traffic yet, which waits on a server anchored first_live_call_received that is still unowned. rows.rationale: The builder's third row was labelled Tools and connectors and held six connector switches and not one tool. It becomes the fourth ResourceField on its own screen: one roster over HTTP tools, the single connector the server actually accepts, and a hosted-code row that keeps its place and states why it cannot run, with the create form behind the sheet's Create new door so a tool stays a workspace record attached by id rather than an editor writing onto the agent. That form ends in one primary, Create and test, which creates the tool, calls it with the function input the user bound and prints the endpoint's own JSON, because none of the four vendors lets you prove a no-code HTTP tool works and our own server already answers that call. The design refuses the word Working: a chip reads Test passed, Test failed or Not tested yet, since enable_tools defaults to false and a test only proves the endpoint answered us, never that the agent called it. It also refuses a connector's tool count, health and last-checked time, a duration beside the status code, and a grid of cards the server would reject, because each of those is a value no record on either side holds.
rows.next: OWNER DECISION: does Studio set advanced_features.enable_tools when an agent holds at least one tool, or does the customer set it? The flag defaults to false and the contract says tools are then validated and not invoked. If Studio sets it, the row ships as drawn. If it does not, a tool can pass its test, attach cleanly and still never fire, so the row needs a fourth state before the call rather than after it, and advanced_features is in the Custom config drawer meanwhile so the flag is at least visible. Second, smaller: 868khqaqj, structured outputs as a reusable resource, is assumed to move to 10 · Session & call logs, so nothing is built for it here and direction E is the design if it stays. rows.clickupSays: ClickUp: research WIP (Couchbase, Wave 1) · UI partial (KB upload) · status added

shot.alt: Knowledge row marked in red: Compliance Laws v2 carries an Answering badge, Data Protection Guidelines reads Attached, not read, under the line One base answers each call. Requires Engine to read a second.

rows.rationale: A knowledge base becomes a container: files and a crawled site are sources inside it, each with its own state, its own read date and its own Refresh now, because a crawl, a schedule and a freshness stamp are properties of a source and none of them is a property of a base. The crawl reports a page ledger before it claims anything, kept, skipped and failed, with a reason against every page that did not make it, and an empty crawl reports zero pages rather than a green chip. The row names the base that actually answers and marks every other one "Attached, not read", because attach takes a list while the engine payload carries one kb_id, so today a second base renders identically and is never read. It refuses the three controls the tickets asked for literally: no schedule picker, because no vendor in the set ships one and the interval is a sentence instead; no login field on a crawl, because private pages reach an agent through a connected account and the form says "Public pages only"; and no knowledge base detail page, which would add a second knowledge surface to an IA tension the owner has ruled open. The two retrieval dials move out of the external form, where Save threw them away, to the agent beside the base they read, and they ship with a per-turn chunk list because a threshold with no chunk view is a dial that changes an invisible number.
rows.next: OWNER DECISION: does the Engine take a list of knowledge bases, a kb_ids beside today's single kb_id? If it stays at one, "Attached, not read" is a permanent state, the Answering mark is the whole feature, and the next honest move is to stop a second base attaching at all, which is a one-line change to the attach switch and your call rather than ours. If it becomes many, the knowledge row turns into an ordered list with eligibility rules and the receipt has to name which base each chunk came from, not just which page. Requires Engine, and marked as such on screen: a list of bases in the payload, a source record carrying address, kind, last read and interval, a crawl job with page counts, retrieval settings on the agent, and a per-turn retrieval record so the receipt can appear on a real call instead of only the Test rail. Not built: every freshness stamp, the crawl, the ledger, the weekly switch and the two dials are browser state, and what a crawl costs a customer is unanswered on screen, because nothing has been priced and the alternative to silence is a number we invented.

rows.verdict: Verdict: B, with C's Answering mark and D's per-turn receipt grafted on
learnings: An authenticated source is a connected account, never a credential on a crawl: not one of the five vendors exposes a header, cookie or password on a crawl, so the crawl says "Public pages only" and the write-only secret stays on the vector store.

A crawl fills a container, it does not become one: Retell lists crawled URLs as sources inside one base and an ElevenLabs crawl job fills a folder, so the crawled site joins the uploaded files in one sources list and freshness becomes a per-source stamp.

Refresh is one switch and one button, and the interval is copy rather than a control: every vendor that refreshes either fixes the cadence or keeps it in the API, so this ships as a switch, a Refresh now, a last-read line and a sentence naming the cadence.

The two retrieval dials belong on the agent, and they are dead controls without the chunk view beside them: Retell puts chunks and threshold on the agent and teaches the loop with a per-turn chunk list, so the dials ship with the receipt or they do not ship.

A blocked crawl is the common failure, so the crawl form has to say who is knocking: ElevenLabs publishes its crawler's user agent and names the silent failure, so ours names the crawler and its allowlist line and an empty crawl reports zero pages.

shot.alt: Variables the prompt declares, marked in red: one definition reads the system prompt, the greeting and the failure message together, so first_name and balance are chipped here instead of spoken as raw braces, and one line under them names the single row that owns the values

rows.rationale: One question is asked once, and it is answered beside the thing that supplies the answer: what will the agent know before it opens its mouth. On batch the contact list parses the file the user actually chose, so the count is read off that file and the coverage block names the one column it does not carry, replacing a line that compared the prompt to itself and could print nothing but three of three covered against a constant that spelled the required column phone. On inbound the same question gets one row, Caller context, sitting in the deployment that raises it: it names the tokens it cannot fill, says plainly that Agora starts the call and not your app, and gives the two ways out, in the same row grammar the batch panel already uses. It refuses the three things the audits killed: a source badge nothing in the product observes, a HubSpot caller-number lookup no Agora doc mentions in any state, and a per-variable fallback whose value would reach no agent because template_variables is set on the start call and absent from the update. It also refuses the Contacts page and the write-back column, because a contact store and a write target are the same missing thing, and the three update modes under that column are another vendor's vocabulary with no Agora field beneath them.
rows.next: OWNER DECISION: does labels become a builder-visible field, or stay a hidden field the CRM feature writes? It is listed in reusablePropertyKeys and then removed from configurablePropertyKeys, and it is the only shipped field that carries a record id from the dial into every notification callback. Make it visible and a call row can name the record it touched, so write-back ships next with attribution and the JTBD's last step has somewhere to land. Leave it hidden and every write stays unattributable, so direction E stays cut rather than shipping as a disabled column. The read half ships either way. Not built in this slice, and Requires Engine rather than drawn greyed out: a pre-greeting context call, a caller-number lookup through the connector, the field list a connector will accept on write, and the contact, audience, suppression and cross-session memory store the ticket asks for. learnings: Inbound context is a webhook the customer hosts in three products out of four, each with a published latency budget, so the P0 read half is a declared variable list and a webhook contract rather than a CRM record picker.

The one vendor with a real contact makes the phone number the identity of the row and not one of its variables, so the fixture drops phone for Agora's documented phone_number and the preview's first column becomes the row's key instead of a variable chip.

Nobody shows the builder what the agent will actually know before the call, and Vapi hides the extra columns from its own preview, so the existing coverage check is the thing to keep and extend into a resolved row rather than the thing to replace.

Cross-session memory ships as a visible mapping table and not a store: Retell maps post-call extraction fields into named contact fields with Overwrite, Fill if empty or Merge per row, which means our answer is rows of the data points we already author.

No vendor puts a person between the agent and the CRM write, and the only boundary any of them ships is a field allowlist plus an update mode, so a draft-and-approve queue is a differentiator we argue for on GDPR grounds and not a table stake we are behind on.

rows.name: 22 · Usage, credits & concurrency
rows.clickupSays: ClickUp: research Done (pricing + managed mode) · UI partial · lock on capacity SKUs · status added
rows.jtbd: User wants to understand what they're paying for and buy more capacity themselves.

shot.alt: Concurrent lines at the wall: all 20 lines in use with 214 calls queued, an estimate that shows its own inputs, Ask for more lines beside a first class Keep queuing, and a gauge reading 20 of 20 in use right now, five live calls and fifteen on batch runs.

rows.rationale: The gauge now reads the only concurrency number Agora publishes, 20 calls at once on one App ID, and in use is composed from the calls that exist, five live plus fifteen on batch runs, so the wall is a state a reviewer can finally see instead of a seeded ten nobody reaches. What the design refuses to do is sell. The per line price in the code is a placeholder its own comment admits to and Engine exposes no concurrency field to set, so the sheet quotes no amount, promises no email and ends at the support route the product already ships. It also refuses to put a dollar beside a model name, because Agora charges $0.10 a minute whichever model runs and a cost tab built on vendor list prices was deleted after audit once already. What survives is the one idea no competitor connects: lines change how fast you spend, not how much, so at the wall the control the account often needs is the cap and not more lines, and the four private line counters that made that warning dead collapse into one derivation with one door.
rows.next: OWNER DECISION: is capacity sold, requested, or sales-assisted? This build ships none of the three. It ships the honest floor, which is the published ceiling, the account's position against it and a route to the support form this app already has, because a request path with no endpoint draws a pending state the contract cannot produce and a sold path needs a price finance has not set. Sell it gives the sheet back a number input, a prorated amount and the lines_added fire. Request it gives the same input plus a pending state once there is somewhere for the request to go. Sales-assisted is what ships today, so each answer is a footer change and nothing else on the screen moves. Requires Engine, each named on screen where it can be: a settable concurrency limit, a readable ceiling (Retell's six fields are the ask), a capacity price and purchase path, per agent and per model minutes, multimodal models on a managed key, and the postpaid or new SKU answer for managed billing. Not built, deliberately: credits, because no credits object exists in either codebase or on docs.agora.io; the capacity purchase path; the MLLM meter row; the usage tracking identity; and Archer, which appears three times in this repo, all the same roadmap row, and nowhere in ng-console, so 868khqb6d gets no surface until somebody says what it is. Deferred with owner question 6: the MANAGED_PROVIDERS correction and the usage breakdown's mode column, so no surface here prints a per vendor managed claim. Left as scope, not truth: the Usage page's period select and its Export toast.

secondary.note: LiveKit prints every ceiling as a row carrying its limit, a live peak usage bar reading 0% and 0 of 5 and its own upgrade link, which is the clearest treatment of concurrency in the set, and it costs them the warning: the page says service may be disrupted when limits are exceeded and never offers to tell you first.

secondary.label: Usage, seven sections of minutes and bytes, all zeroed
secondary.note: LiveKit meters agent session minutes, concurrent sessions, telephony, data, rooms, egress and ingress with billable and non billable named separately, and shows no dollars anywhere, so the number you are at and the number you can reach sit on two different pages and never appear side by side.

secondary.note: ElevenLabs puts a Credits and USD switch on the same series and a Billing Windows control that snaps the x axis to an invoice period, which answers what am I charged for without leaving the chart, and it costs them four units for one bill: credits on the conversation, minutes on the plan and dollars on the rate card.

secondary.label: Subscription, concurrency sold as a tier property
secondary.note: ElevenLabs sells concurrency as a plan property, four concurrent calls on Free rising to forty on Business, so the only lever for more capacity is a bigger subscription, and the table under the tiers restates the same $0.08 a minute on every one of them.

rows.verdict: C with D as its second half, corrected to the honesty floor: one capacity object every surface reads, whose only ceiling is the number Agora publishes, and a usage page whose finest grain is an agent in minutes. C and D answer 21 of the 30 audit rows fully and do not overlap once, because C is the acting half of the job and D is the understanding half, and the happy path ends on D's screen. A is refused for teaching a reviewer a price finance never set, and E is refused on the honesty floor, because answering I cannot tell whether credits and balance are the same money by inventing the credits is not answering it.
learnings: The concurrency ceiling is a readable object at four of five vendors, and Retell publishes the exact field list to ask Engine for, which turns the gauge from a picture of an invented ten into a picture of a granted number.

Model-level usage has to be a minutes column and never a money column, because even the vendor where the model genuinely moves the bill keeps usage on model and cost on line item and warns that the two do not reconcile.

The line fee belongs inside the usage breakdown even though it is not metered, because Retell shows concurrency as one of four cost categories, so the rule about lines and the cap is about what the cap governs and not about where the number is shown.
The cap versus capacity warning is the only idea in this feature that no competitor has, and three of its four doors have it switched off.
New batch calls queue and nothing drops or fails is true of nobody else, so the wall stays a designed behaviour and not a purchase prompt.

The x axis ends in May while today is September, so Last 12 months is the wrong twelve months.
Changing the period changes nothing: the select is uncontrolled and the chart always renders the same twelve constants.
Export is a toast saying the feature does not exist, while the live Console already ships CSV export.

Six of the seven quota meters are hand typed constants that will never move.
The meter and the money are two tabs apart, and only the spend card knows the other exists.
The wall never renders in the shipped state, so the best thing in the feature, queue and nothing drops, is unreachable.
The gauge denominator of ten and the sheet price of eight dollars a line are both invented, and the code comments admit both.
Four mounts of one sheet hold four private counters, and the batch door throws its commit away.
Credits is in the feature's name and is not a thing the product has: the real nouns are a balance and two entitlements.
